newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Aide says Milosevic can run for presidency.
newsitem.headline: Aide says Milosevic can run for presidency.

text.p: Serbia's opposition on Wednesday attacked a government minister's assertion that President Slobodan Milosevic could seek a third term although the constitution limits him to two.

Deputy Prime Minister and lawyer Ratko Markovic told the pro-government daily Politika Ekspres that Milosevic could run for re-election because he served only two years of his first five-year term before calling early elections in 1992.
Milosevic called the elections to consolidate his authority in the face of condemnation at home and abroad over Serbia's role in the outbreak of the Bosnian war earlier in the year.
Serbian presidential and parliamentary elections are due by the end of 1997.
Officials of the divided Zajedno opposition coalition accused Markovic of misreading the law and said Milosevic would violate the constitution by running for re-election.

"If President Milosevic cared at all about Serbia's reputation and credibility he would not even think about a third mandate in an obvious violation of the constitution," Belgrade Mayor and Democratic Party leader Zoran Djindjic said.
Diplomats have speculated that Milosevic would prefer to take over the Yugoslav federal presidency and vest it with new executive powers when it falls vacant in June.

But this option may have been blocked by Montenegro, Serbia's partner in Yugoslavia, whose Prime Minister Milo Djukanovic objected to any change in the largely ceremonial status of the federal presidency.
Markovic's statement indicated that Milosevic may have decided to gamble on retaining the Serbian presidency despite a collapse in his popularity ratings.
Support for his ruling Socialist Party (SPS) plunged in November when it lost control to Zajedno of Serbia's 14 biggest cities, including Belgrade, in local elections.
Milosevic refused to recognise Zajedno victories but three months later he caved in to continuous street demonstrations and intense international pressure.
In February, for the first time since he came to power, Milosevic trailed another politician, Djindjic, in popularity polls.
According to a poll published last week, Zajedno was favoured by 21.6 percent of those questioned against 14.9 percent for the SPS.

Personal disputes within Zajedno, culminating in Serbian Renewal Movement president Vuk Draskovic's nomination for the Serbian presidency, now threaten to sunder the coalition and improve Milosevic's hopes of victory.
"Zajedno is the only hope the Serbian opposition has of ever beating Milosevic. They can take him on only if they are united. Disunited they do not stand a chance," a Western diplomat said.
